claim: Mice deficient for the heme transporter SLC48A1 accumulate over ten-fold excess heme in reticuloendothelial macrophage lysosomes.
source: Here we show that mice deficient for the heme transporter SLC48A1 (also known as HRG1) accumulate over ten-fold excess heme in reticuloendothelial macrophage lysosomes that are 10 to 100 times larger than normal.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing heme accumulation in KO mice through UPLC and ICP-MS measurements (Figure 3D, Figure 5H).

claim: Reticuloendothelial macrophage lysosomes in SLC48A1-deficient mice are 10 to 100 times larger than normal.
source: Here we show that mice deficient for the heme transporter SLC48A1 (also known as HRG1) accumulate over ten-fold excess heme in reticuloendothelial macrophage lysosomes that are 10 to 100 times larger than normal.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images and quantification showing enlarged LAMP1-positive vesicles in KO macrophages (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Macrophages in SLC48A1-deficient mice tolerate high concentrations of heme by crystallizing them into hemozoin.
source: Macrophages tolerate these high concentrations of heme by crystallizing them into hemozoin, which heretofore has only been found in blood-feeding organisms.
evidence: The manuscript provides X-ray powder diffraction data, SEM images, and spectroscopic analysis confirming hemozoin formation (Figure 5F-I).

claim: Hemozoin has only been found in blood-feeding organisms prior to this study.
source: Macrophages tolerate these high concentrations of heme by crystallizing them into hemozoin, which heretofore has only been found in blood-feeding organisms.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on hemozoin in blood-feeding parasites and states this is the first documentation in mammals.

claim: SLC48A1 deficiency results in impaired erythroid maturation.
source: SLC48A1 deficiency results in impaired erythroid maturation and an inability to systemically respond to iron deficiency.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shows increased basophilic erythroblasts (population II) in KO bone marrow (Figure 2A-C).

claim: SLC48A1 deficiency results in an inability to systemically respond to iron deficiency.
source: SLC48A1 deficiency results in impaired erythroid maturation and an inability to systemically respond to iron deficiency.
evidence: The manuscript shows KO mice on low-iron diet have attenuated stress erythropoiesis response and dysregulated iron metabolism genes (Figure 4F-L).

claim: Haplo insufficiency of HMOX1 combined with SLC48A1 inactivation causes perinatal lethality.
source: Complete heme tolerance requires a fully-operational heme degradation pathway as haplo insufficiency of HMOX1 combined with SLC48A1 inactivation causes perinatal lethality demonstrating synthetic lethal interactions between heme transport and degradation.
evidence: Genetic crosses show almost 40% embryonic lethality in HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).

claim: There are synthetic lethal interactions between heme transport and degradation.
source: Complete heme tolerance requires a fully-operational heme degradation pathway as haplo insufficiency of HMOX1 combined with SLC48A1 inactivation causes perinatal lethality demonstrating synthetic lethal interactions between heme transport and degradation.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates that partial reduction of HMOX1 in the absence of SLC48A1 increases perinatal lethality (Figure 6F).

claim: Free heme is cytotoxic as exemplified by hemolytic diseases and genetic deficiencies in heme recycling and detoxifying pathways.
source: Free heme is cytotoxic as exemplified by hemolytic diseases and genetic deficiencies in heme recycling and detoxifying pathways.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on heme cytotoxicity and discusses genetic ablation of HMOX1 causing embryonic lethality.

claim: Intracellular accumulation of heme has not been observed in mammalian cells prior to this study.
source: Thus, intracellular accumulation of heme has not been observed in mammalian cells to date.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge and presents their findings as novel.

claim: Hemolysis can arise from genetic mutations.
source: Hemolysis can arise from genetic mutations (Larsen et al., 2012), parasitic and bacterial infections (Orf and Cunnington, 2015), and drug-induced autoimmune reactions (Garratty, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Larsen et al., 2012 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemolysis can arise from parasitic and bacterial infections.
source: Hemolysis can arise from genetic mutations (Larsen et al., 2012), parasitic and bacterial infections (Orf and Cunnington, 2015), and drug-induced autoimmune reactions (Garratty, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Orf and Cunnington, 2015 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemolysis can arise from drug-induced autoimmune reactions.
source: Hemolysis can arise from genetic mutations (Larsen et al., 2012), parasitic and bacterial infections (Orf and Cunnington, 2015), and drug-induced autoimmune reactions (Garratty, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Garratty, 2009 as support for this claim.

claim: Rupturing of red blood cells releases high concentrations of heme.
source: Rupturing of red blood cells (RBCs) releases high concentrations of heme, which promotes reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Fibach and Rachmilewitz, 2008) and inflammation (Dutra et al., 2014) causing tissue damage and death.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Heme promotes reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.
source: Rupturing of red blood cells (RBCs) releases high concentrations of heme, which promotes reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Fibach and Rachmilewitz, 2008) and inflammation (Dutra et al., 2014) causing tissue damage and death.
evidence: The manuscript cites Fibach and Rachmilewitz, 2008 as support for this claim.

claim: Heme promotes inflammation causing tissue damage and death.
source: Rupturing of red blood cells (RBCs) releases high concentrations of heme, which promotes reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Fibach and Rachmilewitz, 2008) and inflammation (Dutra et al., 2014) causing tissue damage and death.
evidence: The manuscript cites Dutra et al., 2014 as support for this claim.

claim: Genetic ablation of HMOX1 results in >90% embryonic lethality.
source: Consistent with the cytotoxicity of heme, genetic ablation of the heme degrading enzyme, heme oxygenase 1 (HMOX1), results in >90% embryonic lethality (Kovtunovych et al., 2010; Poss and Tonegawa, 1997a; Poss and Tonegawa, 1997b).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kovtunovych et al., 2010; Poss and Tonegawa, 1997a; Poss and Tonegawa, 1997b as support for this claim.

claim: HMOX1 knockout mice that survive are susceptible to hemolytic infections.
source: The few mice that survive are susceptible to hemolytic infections (Seixas et al., 2009), and have little or no reticuloendothelial macrophages (Kovtunovych et al., 2010), a phenotype attributed to heme cytotoxicity.
evidence: The manuscript cites Seixas et al., 2009 as support for this claim.

claim: HMOX1 knockout mice that survive have little or no reticuloendothelial macrophages.
source: The few mice that survive are susceptible to hemolytic infections (Seixas et al., 2009), and have little or no reticuloendothelial macrophages (Kovtunovych et al., 2010), a phenotype attributed to heme cytotoxicity.
evidence: The manuscript cites Kovtunovych et al., 2010 as support for this claim.

claim: Each RBC contains over one billion heme molecules.
source: The majority of body heme is encapsulated within RBCs, and each RBC contains over one billion heme molecules.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Senescent or damaged RBCs are engulfed by macrophages from the reticuloendothelial system through erythrophagocytosis.
source: As RBCs undergo senescence or become damaged, they are engulfed by macrophages from the reticuloendothelial system (RES) through a process termed erythrophagocytosis (EP) (Ganz, 2012; Ganz and Nemeth, 2006; Klei et al., 2017; Winter et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ganz, 2012; Ganz and Nemeth, 2006; Klei et al., 2017; Winter et al., 2014 as support for this claim.

claim: Transporters for heme and non-heme iron are recruited to erythrophagosomal membranes.
source: As RBCs contain both heme and non-heme iron, transporters for each metabolite are recruited to the erythrophagosomal membranes (Delaby et al., 2012; Soe-Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Delaby et al., 2012; Soe-Lin et al., 2010 as support for this claim.

claim: HRG1/SLC48A1 transports heme from the erythrophagosome into the cytosol.
source: The heme responsive gene-1 (HRG1/SLC48A1) transports heme from the erythrophagosome into the cytosol (Rajagopal et al., 2008; White et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Rajagopal et al., 2008; White et al., 2013 as support for this claim.

claim: Heme is enzymatically degraded by HMOX1 to liberate iron.
source: Heme is enzymatically degraded by HMOX1 (Kovtunovych et al., 2010; Kovtunovych et al., 2014) to liberate iron, which can either be stored in ferritin (FTH1) or exported out of the cell by ferroportin (SLC40A1) to be reutilized for new RBC production (Knutson et al., 2005; Knutson et al., 2003), including developing erythroblasts in the bone marrow (Raja et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kovtunovych et al., 2010; Kovtunovych et al., 2014 as support for this claim.

claim: Liberated iron can be stored in ferritin (FTH1) or exported by ferroportin (SLC40A1).
source: Heme is enzymatically degraded by HMOX1 (Kovtunovych et al., 2010; Kovtunovych et al., 2014) to liberate iron, which can either be stored in ferritin (FTH1) or exported out of the cell by ferroportin (SLC40A1) to be reutilized for new RBC production (Knutson et al., 2005; Knutson et al., 2003), including developing erythroblasts in the bone marrow (Raja et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites Knutson et al., 2005; Knutson et al., 2003; Raja et al., 1999 as support for this claim.

claim: Excess heme is exported from the cell by FLVCR1 to prevent heme toxicity.
source: Excess heme is exported from the cell by feline leukemia virus subgroup C cellular receptor 1 (FLVCR1) to prevent heme toxicity (Keel et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites Keel et al., 2008 as support for this claim.

claim: Genetic disruption in HMOX1, SLC40A1, FTH1, and FLVCR1 causes embryonic lethality in mice.
source: Consequently, genetic disruption in HMOX1, SLC40A1, FTH1, and FLVCR1 - steps in the heme-iron recycling pathway - causes embryonic lethality in mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Mice lacking SLC48A1 are viable despite accumulating high concentrations of heme.
source: Here, we show that mice lacking the heme transporter SLC48A1 are viable despite accumulating high concentrations of heme.
evidence: The manuscript shows KO mice are born at Mendelian ratios and survive on standard diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: SLC48A1-deficient mice sequester heme within enlarged lysosomes in RES macrophages.
source: These animals are heme tolerant because they sequester heme within enlarged lysosomes in the RES macrophages and form crystalline hemozoin, which heretofore has only been found in blood-feeding organisms (Shio et al., 2010; Toh et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript provides TEM and confocal microscopy data showing heme sequestration in enlarged LAMP1-positive vesicles (Figure 5J-K).

claim: SLC48A1-deficient mice form crystalline hemozoin.
source: These animals are heme tolerant because they sequester heme within enlarged lysosomes in the RES macrophages and form crystalline hemozoin, which heretofore has only been found in blood-feeding organisms (Shio et al., 2010; Toh et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript provides X-ray powder diffraction, SEM, and spectroscopic data confirming hemozoin formation (Figure 5F-I).

claim: Guide RNAs targeting exon 1 of mouse SLC48A1 produced seven mutant alleles in C57BL/6J × 129/SvJ F1 animals.
source: Guide RNAs targeting exon 1 of mouse SLC48A1 (Figure 1A) produced seven mutant alleles in C57BL/6J × 129/SvJ F1 animals (Table 1 in Supplementary file 1) which were backcrossed to C57BL/6J mice before intercrossing.
evidence: The manuscript describes the CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing approach and references Table 1 in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The M6 allele contains a two base-pair deletion in exon 1 of SLC48A1.
source: We observed similar phenotypes in all mutant alleles and focused on the M6 allele which contains a two base-pair deletion in exon 1 of SLC48A1 (M6).
evidence: The manuscript shows the sequencing chromatogram confirming the two base-pair deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The two base-pair deletion in the M6 allele causes a frameshift within the thirty-third codon immediately after the first transmembrane domain.
source: This deletion causes a frameshift within the thirty-third codon immediately after the first transmembrane domain (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript shows the predicted topology with the frameshift location (Figure 1B).

claim: Intercrossing SLC48A1 HET animals produced KO animals with the expected Mendelian ratio.
source: Intercrossing SLC48A1 HET animals produced KO (knockout) animals with the expected Mendelian ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript shows the Mendelian distribution data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: SLC48A1 mRNA was still detected in KO mice.
source: While SLC48A1 mRNA was still detected (not shown), immunoblots and immunohistochemistry of KO RES tissues showed no detectable SLC48A1 protein, compared to WT (wildtype) tissues which express abundant SLC48A1 (Figure 1C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation directly.

claim: KO RES tissues showed no detectable SLC48A1 protein.
source: While SLC48A1 mRNA was still detected (not shown), immunoblots and immunohistochemistry of KO RES tissues showed no detectable SLC48A1 protein, compared to WT (wildtype) tissues which express abundant SLC48A1 (Figure 1C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The manuscript shows immunoblots and immunohistochemistry data (Figure 1C-D).

claim: KO mice had significantly larger spleens than WT mice.
source: KO mice had significantly larger spleens and lower hematocrits (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript shows spleen weight measurements (Figure 1E).

claim: KO mice had lower hematocrits than WT mice.
source: KO mice had significantly larger spleens and lower hematocrits (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript shows hematocrit measurements (Figure 1F).

claim: Six-week old KO mice revealed darkened spleen, bone marrow, and liver.
source: Gross morphological examination of six-week old KO mice revealed darkened spleen, bone marrow, and liver (Figure 1G) that corresponded with dark intracellular pigments in histochemical tissue sections (Figure 1D, right panel).
evidence: The manuscript shows images of darkened organs (Figure 1G).

claim: Dark intracellular pigments were observed in histochemical tissue sections of KO mice.
source: Gross morphological examination of six-week old KO mice revealed darkened spleen, bone marrow, and liver (Figure 1G) that corresponded with dark intracellular pigments in histochemical tissue sections (Figure 1D, right panel).
evidence: The manuscript shows histochemical images with dark pigments (Figure 1D).

claim: An enlarged spleen is a common hallmark of ineffective and stress erythropoiesis.
source: An enlarged spleen is a common hallmark of ineffective and stress erythropoiesis (Lenox et al., 2005; Perry et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lenox et al., 2005; Perry et al., 2009 as support for this claim.

claim: KO mice had fewer total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow.
source: Consistent with the reduced hematocrits, KO mice had fewer total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow but more basophilic erythroblasts (population II) which are symptomatic of an impairment in erythroid maturation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 2B).

claim: KO mice had more basophilic erythroblasts (population II) in the bone marrow.
source: Consistent with the reduced hematocrits, KO mice had fewer total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow but more basophilic erythroblasts (population II) which are symptomatic of an impairment in erythroid maturation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 2C).

claim: Increased basophilic erythroblasts (population II) are symptomatic of an impairment in erythroid maturation.
source: Consistent with the reduced hematocrits, KO mice had fewer total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow but more basophilic erythroblasts (population II) which are symptomatic of an impairment in erythroid maturation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the flow cytometry data.

claim: KO animals showed significantly more immature erythroid precursor cells (population II+III) in the spleen.
source: In the spleen, despite similar numbers of total Ter-119+ cells (Figure 2D,E), KO animals showed significantly more immature erythroid precursor cells (population II+III), suggesting compensatory erythropoiesis in the spleen (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 2F).

claim: Increased immature erythroid precursor cells in the spleen suggests compensatory erythropoiesis.
source: In the spleen, despite similar numbers of total Ter-119+ cells (Figure 2D,E), KO animals showed significantly more immature erythroid precursor cells (population II+III), suggesting compensatory erythropoiesis in the spleen (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the flow cytometry data.

claim: SLC48A1 is primarily expressed in RES macrophages.
source: Since SLC48A1 is primarily expressed in RES macrophages (White et al., 2013), we analyzed red pulp macrophages (RPMs), which are the primary iron-recycling macrophages in the spleen (Beaumont and Delaby, 2009; Ganz and Nemeth, 2012; Haldar et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites White et al., 2013 as support for this claim.

claim: Red pulp macrophages (RPMs) are the primary iron-recycling macrophages in the spleen.
source: Since SLC48A1 is primarily expressed in RES macrophages (White et al., 2013), we analyzed red pulp macrophages (RPMs), which are the primary iron-recycling macrophages in the spleen (Beaumont and Delaby, 2009; Ganz and Nemeth, 2012; Haldar et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Beaumont and Delaby, 2009; Ganz and Nemeth, 2012; Haldar et al., 2014 as support for this claim.

claim: Significantly fewer mature RPMs (F4/80hiTreml4+) were detected in KO spleens.
source: Significantly fewer mature RPMs (F4/80hiTreml4+) were detected in KO spleens (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) which correlated with increased numbers of immature RPMs by ratiometric quantification of monocytes (F4/80int: F4/80lo-CD11bhi) (Figure 2I,J; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 2H).

claim: Reduced mature RPMs in KO spleens correlated with increased numbers of immature RPMs.
source: Significantly fewer mature RPMs (F4/80hiTreml4+) were detected in KO spleens (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) which correlated with increased numbers of immature RPMs by ratiometric quantification of monocytes (F4/80int: F4/80lo-CD11bhi) (Figure 2I,J; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 2J).

claim: KO mice on a standard diet (380 ppm Fe) have normal serum iron, TIBC and transferrin saturation.
source: KO mice on a standard diet (380 ppm Fe) have normal serum iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) and transferrin saturation but significantly elevated serum ferritin, an indicator of tissue iron-overload (Ganz and Nemeth, 2012) (Table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript references Table 2 in Supplementary file 1 with serum analysis data.

claim: KO mice on a standard diet have significantly elevated serum ferritin.
source: KO mice on a standard diet (380 ppm Fe) have normal serum iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) and transferrin saturation but significantly elevated serum ferritin, an indicator of tissue iron-overload (Ganz and Nemeth, 2012) (Table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript references Table 2 in Supplementary file 1 with serum analysis data.

claim: Elevated serum ferritin is an indicator of tissue iron-overload.
source: KO mice on a standard diet (380 ppm Fe) have normal serum iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) and transferrin saturation but significantly elevated serum ferritin, an indicator of tissue iron-overload (Ganz and Nemeth, 2012) (Table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ganz and Nemeth, 2012 as support for this claim.

claim: In situ Perls' Prussian blue staining did not show significant differences in iron deposition in tissue biopsies between WT and KO mice.
source: However, in situ Perls' Prussian blue staining did not show significant differences in iron deposition in tissue biopsies (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript shows Perls' Prussian blue staining images (Figure 3B).

claim: Dark pigments may have masked the visualization of the Prussian blue iron complex.
source: Because it is possible that the dark pigments masked the visualization of the Prussian blue iron complex, we performed inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to measure total metal content.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the Prussian blue staining results.

claim: Significantly more iron was found in the spleens, livers and bone marrows of KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Significantly more iron was found in the spleens, livers and bone marrows of KO mice (Figure 3C), as compared to copper, zinc, and manganese (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D); a modest 1.4-fold change in manganese was observed in the spleens of KO mice in contrast to 2-fold increase in iron (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript shows ICP-MS data (Figure 3C).

claim: KO spleens and bone marrows had significantly more total heme (10-fold and 3-fold, respectively) than WT organs.
source: Through a combination of ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) (Sinclair et al., 2001) and ICP-MS to measure heme-iron and total iron, we observed that KO spleens and bone marrows had significantly more total heme (10-fold and 3-fold, respectively) than WT organs (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), which indicates that the higher iron content observed in these tissues is due to the accumulation of heme.
evidence: The manuscript shows UPLC and ICP-MS data (Figure 3D).

claim: The higher iron content observed in KO tissues is due to the accumulation of heme.
source: Through a combination of ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) (Sinclair et al., 2001) and ICP-MS to measure heme-iron and total iron, we observed that KO spleens and bone marrows had significantly more total heme (10-fold and 3-fold, respectively) than WT organs (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), which indicates that the higher iron content observed in these tissues is due to the accumulation of heme.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the UPLC and ICP-MS data.

claim: Dark inclusions were found in F4/80+ cells in all three RES tissues of KO mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry using a macrophage-specific antibody showed dark inclusions in F4/80+ cells in all three RES tissues (Figure 3E, right panel arrows, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: The manuscript shows immunohistochemistry images (Figure 3E).

claim: KO macrophages contained significantly higher concentrations of cellular iron than WT macrophages.
source: Overall, KO macrophages contained significantly higher concentrations of cellular iron (Figure 3F,G), copper, sulfur, and calcium (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript shows XFM data (Figure 3G).

claim: Iron was the most abundant trace element within the dark pigments in KO macrophages.
source: However, region-of-interest (ROI) quantification around the dark pigments in KO macrophages confirmed that iron was the most abundant trace element within this region (Figure 3H).
evidence: The manuscript shows XFM ROI quantification data (Figure 3H).

claim: Total body iron is a composite of recycled heme-iron from damaged RBCs and dietary iron absorption.
source: Total body iron is a composite of recycled heme-iron from damaged RBCs and dietary iron absorption.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The standard rodent diet contains ≈380 ppm of iron.
source: The standard rodent diet contains ≈380 ppm of iron, which is significantly greater than the amount of iron (25 to 100 ppm) required to sustain normal erythropoiesis and the growth of laboratory mice (Sorbie and Valberg, 1974).
evidence: The manuscript cites Sorbie and Valberg, 1974 as support for this claim.

claim: 25 to 100 ppm of iron is required to sustain normal erythropoiesis and growth of laboratory mice.
source: The standard rodent diet contains ≈380 ppm of iron, which is significantly greater than the amount of iron (25 to 100 ppm) required to sustain normal erythropoiesis and the growth of laboratory mice (Sorbie and Valberg, 1974).
evidence: The manuscript cites Sorbie and Valberg, 1974 as support for this claim.

claim: A significant percentage of KO mice, but not WT mice, died within 20 weeks on the low-iron diet.
source: A significant percentage of KO mice, but not WT mice, died within 20 weeks on the low-iron diet (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript shows Kaplan-Meier survival curve (Figure 4A).

claim: For the first five weeks on low-iron diet, the hematocrits of WT and KO mice are comparable.
source: Importantly, for the first five weeks, the hematocrits of WT and KO mice on the low-iron diet are comparable (Mazzaccara et al., 2008) (Figure 4B), but by 8 weeks the hematocrits of KO mice were significantly lower (p<0.01), and by 20 weeks they were severely anemic (13.2 ± 2.3 KO versus 39.8 ± 2.2 WT, p<0.0001; Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript shows hematocrit data (Figure 4B).

claim: By 8 weeks on low-iron diet, the hematocrits of KO mice were significantly lower than WT mice.
source: Importantly, for the first five weeks, the hematocrits of WT and KO mice on the low-iron diet are comparable (Mazzaccara et al., 2008) (Figure 4B), but by 8 weeks the hematocrits of KO mice were significantly lower (p<0.01), and by 20 weeks they were severely anemic (13.2 ± 2.3 KO versus 39.8 ± 2.2 WT, p<0.0001; Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript shows hematocrit data (Figure 4C).

claim: By 20 weeks on low-iron diet, KO mice were severely anemic.
source: Importantly, for the first five weeks, the hematocrits of WT and KO mice on the low-iron diet are comparable (Mazzaccara et al., 2008) (Figure 4B), but by 8 weeks the hematocrits of KO mice were significantly lower (p<0.01), and by 20 weeks they were severely anemic (13.2 ± 2.3 KO versus 39.8 ± 2.2 WT, p<0.0001; Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript shows hematocrit data (Figure 4C).

claim: The defect in heme-iron recycling in KO mice becomes more pronounced after five weeks on an iron-deficient diet.
source: These results imply that the defect in heme-iron recycling in KO mice becomes more pronounced after five weeks on an iron-deficient diet.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the hematocrit data over time.

claim: Serum ferritin levels remained elevated in KO mice on a low-iron diet.
source: Analyses of serum from iron-deficient animals showed no significant differences in serum iron, TIBC, or transferrin saturation, but serum ferritin levels remained elevated in KO mice on a low-iron diet (Table 2 in Supplementary file 1, 2 ppm diet).
evidence: The manuscript references Table 2 in Supplementary file 1 with serum analysis data.

claim: The levels of iron and heme retained within RES organs of KO mice on low-iron diet were significantly higher than WT mice.
source: The levels of iron and heme retained within RES organs of KO mice were also significantly higher than WT mice (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the heme-iron stores in KO mice were not bioavailable despite systemic iron-deficiency.
evidence: The manuscript shows ICP-MS and UPLC data (Figure 4D-E).

claim: The heme-iron stores in KO mice were not bioavailable despite systemic iron-deficiency.
source: The levels of iron and heme retained within RES organs of KO mice were also significantly higher than WT mice (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the heme-iron stores in KO mice were not bioavailable despite systemic iron-deficiency.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the iron and heme measurement data.

claim: In response to iron deficiency, the spleens of WT mice increased by approximately 120%.
source: In response to iron deficiency, the spleens of WT mice increased by approximately 120% (Figure 4F) (Lenox et al., 2005; Perry et al., 2009; Socolovsky, 2007), with a concomitant increase (7.5-fold) in immature Ter119+ cells, a hallmark of stress erythropoiesis (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The manuscript shows splenomegaly data (Figure 4F) and cites literature on stress erythropoiesis.

claim: WT mice showed a 7.5-fold increase in immature Ter119+ cells in response to iron deficiency, a hallmark of stress erythropoiesis.
source: In response to iron deficiency, the spleens of WT mice increased by approximately 120% (Figure 4F) (Lenox et al., 2005; Perry et al., 2009; Socolovsky, 2007), with a concomitant increase (7.5-fold) in immature Ter119+ cells, a hallmark of stress erythropoiesis (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 4G-H).

claim: The stress erythropoiesis response in iron-deficient KO mice was significantly attenuated.
source: In contrast, the stress erythropoiesis response in iron-deficient KO mice was significantly attenuated (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), with erythroblast differentiation blocked at an earlier stage (population I) in the bone marrow (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript shows splenomegaly and flow cytometry data (Figure 4F-H).

claim: Erythroblast differentiation was blocked at an earlier stage (population I) in the bone marrow of iron-deficient KO mice.
source: In contrast, the stress erythropoiesis response in iron-deficient KO mice was significantly attenuated (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), with erythroblast differentiation blocked at an earlier stage (population I) in the bone marrow (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 4I).

claim: Iron deficiency fully restored the total numbers of mature RPM population in KO mice to WT levels.
source: Iron deficiency fully restored the total numbers of mature RPM population and balance in monocyte populations (Figure 4J,K) in KO mice to WT levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 4J).

claim: Iron deficiency restored the balance in monocyte populations in KO mice to WT levels.
source: Iron deficiency fully restored the total numbers of mature RPM population and balance in monocyte populations (Figure 4J,K) in KO mice to WT levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 4K).

claim: Restoration of RPM populations in iron-deficient KO mice could reflect increased viability of erythrophagocytic RPMs due to reduced heme accumulation under systemic iron deficiency.
source: This could reflect increased viability of erythrophagocytic RPMs due to reduced heme accumulation in these cells under systemic iron deficiency.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the RPM restoration.

claim: Iron-deficient KO mice showed significant dysregulation in 38% of iron/heme metabolism mRNAs in the spleen.
source: Iron-deficient KO mice showed significant dysregulation in 38% and 6% of these mRNAs in the spleen and liver, respectively (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I, and Table 1 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript shows gene expression heatmap and qPCR data (Figure 4L).

claim: Iron-deficient KO mice showed significant dysregulation in 6% of iron/heme metabolism mRNAs in the liver.
source: Iron-deficient KO mice showed significant dysregulation in 38% and 6% of these mRNAs in the spleen and liver, respectively (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I, and Table 1 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript shows gene expression heatmap and qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Under iron-deficient conditions, the levels of 32 iron metabolism mRNAs were significantly reduced in WT spleens but remained high in KO spleens.
source: Under iron-deficient conditions, the levels of 32 iron metabolism mRNAs were significantly reduced in WT spleens (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, compare WT Standard vs WT 2 ppm, KO Standard vs KO 2 ppm), but remained high in KO spleens.
evidence: The manuscript shows qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).

claim: KO mice are unable to respond normally to iron-deficiency, especially at sites where heme-iron accumulates at high levels.
source: Together, these data suggest that KO mice are unable to respond normally to iron-deficiency, especially at sites where heme-iron accumulates at high levels such as the spleen.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the gene expression and physiological data.

claim: The spleens of WT mice accumulated 59Fe within 24 hr followed by a decrease at 96 hr.
source: The spleens of WT mice accumulated 59Fe within 24 hr followed by a decrease at 96 hr with a concomitant increase of 59Fe in the circulation and kidneys (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript shows 59Fe distribution data (Figure 5B).

claim: The spleens of KO mice accumulated more 59Fe over the course of 96 hr with limited amounts of 59Fe in the circulation and kidneys.
source: By contrast, the spleens of KO mice accumulated more 59Fe over the course of 96 hr with limited amounts of 59Fe in the circulation and kidneys, suggesting that the release of 59Fe from phagocytosed RBCs was impaired (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript shows 59Fe distribution data (Figure 5B).

claim: The release of 59Fe from phagocytosed RBCs was impaired in KO mice.
source: By contrast, the spleens of KO mice accumulated more 59Fe over the course of 96 hr with limited amounts of 59Fe in the circulation and kidneys, suggesting that the release of 59Fe from phagocytosed RBCs was impaired (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the 59Fe distribution data.

claim: KO spleens accumulated significantly greater levels of 59Fe compared to WT spleens, primarily due to 59Fe counts within the organic heme fraction.
source: While KO spleens accumulated significantly greater levels of 59Fe compared to WT spleens, these differences were primarily due to 59Fe counts within the organic heme fraction ([59Fe]heme) and not in the aqueous iron fraction (59Fe) (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The manuscript shows differential extraction data (Figure 5C).

claim: A large portion of 59Fe was detected in the detergent-insoluble fraction of KO spleens and livers.
source: A large portion of 59Fe was detected in the detergent-insoluble fraction of KO spleens (Figure 5C) and livers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript shows differential extraction data (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: A proteinase and detergent resistant fraction enriched in iron is characteristic of hemozoin.
source: A proteinase and detergent resistant fraction enriched in iron is characteristic of hemozoin, a crystallized form of heme generated during the digestion of hemoglobin by blood-feeding organisms such as Plasmodium (Egan, 2008; Francis et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Egan, 2008; Francis et al., 1997 as support for this claim.

claim: Spectroscopic analysis of the dissolved detergent-resistant fraction revealed absorption spectra characteristic of heme.
source: Spectroscopic analysis of the dissolved detergent-resistant fraction revealed absorption spectra characteristic of heme (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript shows spectroscopic data (Figure 5E).

claim: High resolution X-ray powder diffraction confirmed that the dark pigment from KO spleens is identical to malarial hemozoin.
source: High resolution X-ray powder diffraction of the purified insoluble fraction from the KO spleens confirmed that the dark pigment is identical to malarial hemozoin (Figure 5F) (Coronado et al., 2014; Slater et al., 1991).
evidence: The manuscript shows X-ray powder diffraction data (Figure 5F) and cites literature on malarial hemozoin structure.

claim: The hemozoin structure reveals a repeating unit of heme dimers linked together by iron-carboxylate bonds to one propionic acid side chain.
source: The structure reveals a repeating unit of heme dimers linked together by iron-carboxylate bonds to one propionic acid side chain with the adjacent heme dimers forming stable chains by hydrogen bonding via the free propionate side chain (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) (Coronado et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript shows the chemical structure (Figure 5G) and cites Coronado et al., 2014.

claim: Adjacent heme dimers form stable chains by hydrogen bonding via the free propionate side chain.
source: The structure reveals a repeating unit of heme dimers linked together by iron-carboxylate bonds to one propionic acid side chain with the adjacent heme dimers forming stable chains by hydrogen bonding via the free propionate side chain (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) (Coronado et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript shows the chemical structure (Figure 5G) and cites Coronado et al., 2014.

claim: Substantial amounts of hemozoin-heme were present in the spleens and livers of KO mice, but not in WT mice.
source: Spectrophotometric analysis of the dissolved hemozoin fractions showed substantial amounts of hemozoin-heme present in the spleens and livers of KO mice, but not in WT mice (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript shows spectrophotometric quantification data (Figure 5H).

claim: A significant amount of heme in non-hemozoin form was found in KO spleens (2-fold of WT).
source: Notably, a significant amount of heme in non-hemozoin form was also found in KO spleens (2-fold of WT; Figure 5H).
evidence: The manuscript shows spectrophotometric quantification data (Figure 5H).

claim: Mammalian hemozoin was heterogeneous in size.
source: Scanning electron microscopy images showed mammalian hemozoin was heterogeneous; purified hemozoin crystals from spleen and liver appeared larger than Plasmodium falciparum hemozoin, while bone marrow-purified hemozoin was similar in size (Figure 5I).
evidence: The manuscript shows SEM images (Figure 5I).

claim: Hemozoin was sequestered within a membrane-enclosed compartment in F4/80+ tissue-resident macrophages.
source: Transmission electron microscopy with purified F4/80+ tissue-resident macrophages from the spleen and bone marrow showed that hemozoin was sequestered within a membrane-enclosed compartment (Figure 5J).
evidence: The manuscript shows TEM images (Figure 5J).

claim: Isolated KO monocytes that were differentiated into macrophages in vitro did not contain any hemozoin.
source: However, isolated KO monocytes that were differentiated into macrophages in vitro did not contain any hemozoin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), indicating that hemozoin formation occurs in vivo after tissue resident macrophages are established.
evidence: The manuscript shows TEM images (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Hemozoin formation occurs in vivo after tissue resident macrophages are established.
source: However, isolated KO monocytes that were differentiated into macrophages in vitro did not contain any hemozoin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), indicating that hemozoin formation occurs in vivo after tissue resident macrophages are established.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the in vitro differentiation data.

claim: All of the hemozoin in isolated-F4/80+ macrophages from KO bone marrow is enclosed within LAMP1-positive compartments.
source: Confocal microscopy using antibodies against LAMP1, which has been previously demonstrated to be a strong marker of erythrophagosomes in macrophages (Delaby et al., 2012; Huynh et al., 2007), showed that all of the hemozoin in isolated-F4/80+ macrophages from KO bone marrow is enclosed within LAMP1-positive compartments (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript shows confocal microscopy images (Figure 5K) and cites literature on LAMP1 as an erythrophagosome marker.

claim: LAMP1 is a strong marker of erythrophagosomes in macrophages.
source: Confocal microscopy using antibodies against LAMP1, which has been previously demonstrated to be a strong marker of erythrophagosomes in macrophages (Delaby et al., 2012; Huynh et al., 2007), showed that all of the hemozoin in isolated-F4/80+ macrophages from KO bone marrow is enclosed within LAMP1-positive compartments (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript cites Delaby et al., 2012; Huynh et al., 2007 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemozoin-containing LAMP1-positive vesicles were significantly larger (diameter 570 to 4300 nm) compared to typical lysosomes which range from 50 nm to 500 nm.
source: Furthermore, these hemozoin-containing LAMP1-positive vesicles were significantly larger (diameter 570 to 4300 nm) compared to typical lysosomes which range from 50 nm to 500 nm (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2014) (Figure 5K, compare vesicles with white vs yellow arrows; Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript shows confocal microscopy images and quantification (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) and cites literature on typical lysosome size.

claim: Intracellular hemozoin is typically known to be inert.
source: Intracellular hemozoin is typically known to be inert and ingested malarial hemozoin can remain unmodified for long periods of time within human monocytes (Schwarzer et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites Schwarzer et al., 1993 as support for this claim.

claim: Ingested malarial hemozoin can remain unmodified for long periods of time within human monocytes.
source: Intracellular hemozoin is typically known to be inert and ingested malarial hemozoin can remain unmodified for long periods of time within human monocytes (Schwarzer et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites Schwarzer et al., 1993 as support for this claim.

claim: RES macrophages were completely depleted by day three post-injection of clodronate liposomes.
source: RES macrophages were completely depleted by day three post-injection but KO spleens, livers and bone marrows still retained hemozoin, which were now extruded into the interstitial space (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the clodronate liposome experiment.

claim: Hemozoin was not bioavailable as an iron source to correct iron deficiency anemia even after seven days following macrophage depletion.
source: However, this hemozoin was not bioavailable as an iron source to correct iron deficiency anemia even after seven days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript shows hematocrit data after clodronate treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).

claim: In the absence of SLC48A1, RES macrophages are unable to recycle and degrade heme from ingested RBC resulting in heme accumulation and biocrystallization into hemozoin within enlarged phagolysosomes.
source: Altogether, these results strongly indicate that in the absence of SLC48A1, RES macrophages are unable to recycle and degrade heme from ingested RBC resulting in heme accumulation and biocrystallization into hemozoin within enlarged phagolysosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the 59Fe labeling and microscopy experiments.

claim: WT and KO BMDMs engulfed similar numbers of opsonized RBCs.
source: Although WT and KO BMDMs engulfed similar numbers of opsonized RBCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), SLC48A1-deficient cells accumulated significantly more heme even after 72 hr post-EP (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript references Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing ROS images.

claim: SLC48A1-deficient cells accumulated significantly more heme even after 72 hr post-EP.
source: Although WT and KO BMDMs engulfed similar numbers of opsonized RBCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), SLC48A1-deficient cells accumulated significantly more heme even after 72 hr post-EP (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript shows heme quantification data (Figure 6A).

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production was significantly lower in KO cells during the early phase (4 hr) of erythrophagocytosis.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Figure 6B) (Delaby et al., 2005; Kovtunovych et al., 2010) and the ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione levels (GSSG:GSH) (Figure 6C) was significantly lower in KO cells during the early phase, when active digestion of red cells takes place.
evidence: The manuscript shows ROS quantification data (Figure 6B).

claim: The ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione levels (GSSG:GSH) was significantly lower in KO cells during the early phase of erythrophagocytosis.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Figure 6B) (Delaby et al., 2005; Kovtunovych et al., 2010) and the ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione levels (GSSG:GSH) (Figure 6C) was significantly lower in KO cells during the early phase, when active digestion of red cells takes place.
evidence: The manuscript shows GSSG:GSH ratio data (Figure 6C).

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release into the growth medium was significantly reduced in KO cells in the late phase (24 hr) of erythrophagocytosis.
source: Consistent with this early suppression of ROS, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release into the growth medium (Rayamajhi et al., 2013) was also significantly reduced in KO cells in the late phase (Figure 6D), with no loss in cell adherence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) (Delaby et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript shows LDH release data (Figure 6D).

claim: SLC48A1 deficiency protects the macrophages from the damaging effects of erythrophagocytosis.
source: Together, these results imply that SLC48A1 deficiency protects the macrophages from the damaging effects of EP (Delaby et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ROS, GSSG:GSH, and LDH data.

claim: HMOX1 induction and abundance were comparable between WT and KO BMDMs over 72 hr post-EP.
source: However, EP studies reveal that HMOX1 induction and abundance were comparable between WT and KO BMDMs over 72 hr post-EP (Figure 6E)
evidence: The manuscript shows immunoblot data (Figure 6E).

claim: In the absence of SLC48A1, an alternate albeit less-efficient heme transport pathway could translocate heme from the phagolyosome for degradation by HMOX1.
source: These results raised the possibility that, in the absence of SLC48A1, an alternate albeit less-efficient heme transport pathway could translocate heme from the phagolyosome for degradation by HMOX1.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the HMOX1 induction data.

claim: Analysis of offspring from HMOX1 HET and HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO intercrosses showed reduced numbers of viable HMOX1 KO progeny regardless of the presence of SLC48A1.
source: Analysis of offspring from HMOX1 HET and HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO intercrosses showed reduced numbers of viable HMOX1 KO progeny (Observed/Expected: HMOX1 KO 9/64 versus DKO 9/86) regardless of the presence of SLC48A1 (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript shows genetic cross data (Figure 6F).

claim: HMOX1 KO and DKO mice showed similar reductions in RES macrophages and erythropoietic profiles from the bone marrow and spleen at ten weeks of age.
source: Consistent with this observation, HMOX1 KO and DKO mice showed similar reductions in RES macrophages and erythropoietic profiles from the bone marrow and spleen at ten weeks of age (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–I), and developed anemia as they grew older (not shown).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-I).

claim: Heterozygous offspring from HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO intercrosses showed almost 40% embryonic lethality.
source: Unexpectedly, heterozygous offspring from HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO intercrosses did not show Mendelian ratio at birth, with almost 40% embryonic lethality (Observed/Expected: HMOX1 HET 133/128 versus HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO 108/172) (p<0.001 by chi-square test) (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript shows genetic cross data (Figure 6F).

claim: HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice showed an enhanced reduction in splenic RPMs compared to HMOX1 HET mice.
source: Flow cytometry analyses of HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice showed an enhanced reduction in splenic RPMs (Figure 6G) and total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow (Figure 6H) compared to HMOX1 HET mice.
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 6G).

claim: HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice showed an enhanced reduction in total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow compared to HMOX1 HET mice.
source: Flow cytometry analyses of HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice showed an enhanced reduction in splenic RPMs (Figure 6G) and total Ter-119+ cells in the bone marrow (Figure 6H) compared to HMOX1 HET mice.
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 6H).

claim: The bone marrow subpopulations of Ter-119+ cells were significantly reduced in populations II to V in HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice.
source: The bone marrow subpopulations of Ter-119+ cells were also significantly reduced in populations II to V in HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 6I).

claim: The spleens of HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice had fewer Ter-119+ cells with more immature Ter-119+ cells.
source: The spleens of HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice had fewer Ter-119+ cells with more immature Ter-119+ cells (Figure 6J,K), suggesting ineffective stress erythropoiesis.
evidence: The manuscript shows flow cytometry data (Figure 6J-K).

claim: Partial reduction or haploinsufficiency of HMOX1 in the absence of SLC48A1 increases perinatal lethality and a shift to synthetic lethality.
source: Together these results reveal that inhibition of HMOX1 in the absence of SLC48A1 has two different outcomes depending on the degree of HMOX1 impairment. Partial reduction or haploinsufficiency of HMOX1, as observed in HMOX1 HET; SLC48A1 KO mice, increases perinatal lethality and a shift to synthetic lethality.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the genetic cross and phenotypic data.

claim: Complete inhibition of HMOX1 leads to loss in cell viability and greater embryonic mortality of DKO and HMOX1 KO mice.
source: However, complete inhibition of HMOX1 leads to loss in cell viability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J,K) and greater embryonic mortality of DKO and HMOX1 KO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating a delicate balance between heme transport and degradation.
evidence: The manuscript shows LDH data and genetic cross data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J-K, C).

claim: There is a delicate balance between heme transport and degradation.
source: However, complete inhibition of HMOX1 leads to loss in cell viability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J,K) and greater embryonic mortality of DKO and HMOX1 KO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating a delicate balance between heme transport and degradation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the genetic and cell viability data.

claim: KO mice are defective in transporting heme across the phagosomal membrane during erythrophagocytosis.
source: Our results show that (SLC48A1) KO mice are defective in transporting heme across the phagosomal membrane during EP, resulting in large amounts of heme accumulation and hemozoin formation within phagolysosomes of RES macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the 59Fe labeling and microscopy experiments.

claim: Heme retention in KO mice leads to impaired iron recycling for erythrocyte production in the bone marrow.
source: Heme retention leads to impaired iron recycling for erythrocyte production in the bone marrow, stimulating extramedullary erythropoiesis similar to the effects caused by iron-deficiency (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the erythroid profiling data.

claim: The overall impact on RBC production and anemia is modest on a standard iron diet (380 ppm).
source: However, the overall impact on RBC production and anemia is modest on a standard iron diet (380 ppm).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the hematocrit data on standard diet.

claim: Mice on an iron-rich diet can circumvent a block in heme-iron recycling by relying more heavily on dietary iron for erythropoiesis.
source: These findings support the conclusion that mice on an iron-rich diet can circumvent a block in heme-iron recycling by relying more heavily on dietary iron for erythropoiesis (Ganz and Nemeth, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the dietary iron studies and cites Ganz and Nemeth, 2006.

claim: In humans, daily iron absorption does not exceed 10% of the amount of recycled iron utilized for erythropoiesis.
source: This is in stark contrast to humans where the daily iron absorption does not exceed 10% of the amount of recycled iron utilized for erythropoiesis (Kautz and Nemeth, 2014; Muñoz et al., 2009; Winter et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kautz and Nemeth, 2014; Muñoz et al., 2009; Winter et al., 2014 as support for this claim.

claim: When KO mice are fed a low-iron diet, the block in heme-iron recycling is exacerbated.
source: However, when KO mice are fed a low-iron diet, the block in heme-iron recycling is exacerbated.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the low-iron diet studies.

claim: It takes approximately eight weeks for body iron stores to be depleted in the absence of heme-iron recycling.
source: Furthermore, when KO mice encounter prolonged dietary iron limitation (8 to 20 weeks), they are unable to sustain erythropoiesis, implying that it takes approximately eight weeks for body iron stores to be depleted in the absence of heme-iron recycling.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the hematocrit data over time on low-iron diet.

claim: The relative proportion of 59Fe retained within the spleens of KO mice are 50.3% hemozoin: 34.4% heme: 15.3% non-heme iron after 96 hr.
source: Indeed, results from the in vivo 59Fe-labeled RBC studies show that the relative proportion of 59Fe retained within the spleens of KO mice are 50.3% hemozoin: 34.4% heme: 15.3% non-heme iron after 96 hr (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript shows differential extraction data (Figure 5C).

claim: Assuming ineffective heme-iron recycling reduces recycled iron according to the law of exponential decay and RBCs have a lifespan of ~40 days, the 59Fe distribution pattern would predict that KO mice would become significantly anemic after six weeks as hemozoin accumulates after RBC turnover.
source: Assuming that ineffective heme-iron recycling reduces recycled iron according to the law of exponential decay (Leike, 2002) and RBCs have a lifespan of ~40 days, this 59Fe distribution pattern would predict that KO mice would become significantly anemic after six weeks as hemozoin accumulates after RBC turnover.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on mathematical modeling and cites Leike, 2002.

claim: The KO mice were developed on a mixed genetic background (75% C57BL/6J, 25% 129/SvJ).
source: Another potential contributing factor is the mouse genetic background. The KO mice were developed on a mixed genetic background (75% C57BL/6J, 25% 129/SvJ).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the mouse strain.

claim: 129/SvJ mice have more hepatic iron stores than C57BL/6J mice on an iron-balanced diet.
source: Published studies comparing the iron status of C57BL/6J and 129/SvJ mice on an iron-balanced diet have shown that 129/SvJ mice have more hepatic iron stores (Dupic et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Dupic et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2007 as support for this claim.

claim: KO C57BL/6J mice showed severe anemia within 5.5 weeks on iron-deficient diet compared to WT littermate controls.
source: We recently generated KO mice on a pure C57BL/6J background and placed these mice on an iron-deficient diet post-weaning (P21). KO C57BL/6J mice showed severe anemia within 5.5 weeks compared to WT littermate controls, which approximates one lifespan of circulating erythrocytes (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from a recent experiment.

claim: Genetic strain differences that influence body iron stores are important modifiers of the SLC48A1 mutant phenotype.
source: This result indicates that genetic strain differences that influence body iron stores are important modifiers of the SLC48A1 mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the genetic background experiments.

claim: KO mice reach a 'metabolic threshold' on a low-iron diet, that is a physiological transition from an intermediate iron state to severe iron limitation.
source: Taken together, we conclude that KO mice reach a 'metabolic threshold' on a low-iron diet, that is a physiological transition from an intermediate iron state to severe iron limitation, which eventually lead to mortality in these animals (Figure 6L, right panel).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the dietary iron studies.

claim: Under iron-deficient conditions, the production of the liver hormone hepcidin is suppressed.
source: Typically under iron-deficient conditions, the production of the liver hormone hepcidin is suppressed, which results in greater mobilization of iron by SLC40A1 to iron-deprived compartments (Ganz and Nemeth, 2006; Nemeth et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ganz and Nemeth, 2006; Nemeth et al., 2004 as support for this claim.

claim: Suppression of hepcidin results in greater mobilization of iron by SLC40A1 to iron-deprived compartments.
source: Typically under iron-deficient conditions, the production of the liver hormone hepcidin is suppressed, which results in greater mobilization of iron by SLC40A1 to iron-deprived compartments (Ganz and Nemeth, 2006; Nemeth et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ganz and Nemeth, 2006; Nemeth et al., 2004 as support for this claim.

claim: The inability to sustain erythropoiesis, despite significant suppression in hepatic hepcidin expression in KO iron-deficient mice, suggests that systemic iron status is uncoupled from tissue and cellular iron status in the absence of SLC48A1.
source: The inability to sustain erythropoiesis, despite a significant suppression in hepatic hepcidin expression in KO iron-deficient mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), suggest that these mice are iron-deprived even though the RES tissues are heme-iron loaded, that is systemic iron status is uncoupled from tissue and cellular iron status in the absence of SLC48A1.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the gene expression and physiological data.

claim: Hepatic hepcidin is considered to be the major facilitator of systemic iron homeostasis.
source: While hepatic hepcidin is considered to be the major facilitator of systemic iron homeostasis, recent studies have uncovered an autocrine role for locally-produced hepcidin in regulating cardiac iron homeostasis (Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and cites Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2016 for the autocrine role.

claim: Recent studies have uncovered an autocrine role for locally-produced hepcidin in regulating cardiac iron homeostasis.
source: While hepatic hepcidin is considered to be the major facilitator of systemic iron homeostasis, recent studies have uncovered an autocrine role for locally-produced hepcidin in regulating cardiac iron homeostasis (Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2016 as support for this claim.

claim: KO mice show elevated splenic hepcidin regardless of iron status.
source: Indeed, KO mice show elevated splenic hepcidin regardless of iron status (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), implying a role for splenic hepcidin in stress erythropoiesis.
evidence: The manuscript shows qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Elevated splenic hepcidin in KO mice implies a role for splenic hepcidin in stress erythropoiesis.
source: Indeed, KO mice show elevated splenic hepcidin regardless of iron status (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), implying a role for splenic hepcidin in stress erythropoiesis.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the splenic hepcidin expression data.

claim: Heme-iron recycling of senescent erythrocytes occurs in the RES macrophages - mainly in the splenic RPMs and, to some extent, in liver Kupffer cells and bone marrow macrophages.
source: Heme-iron recycling of senescent erythrocytes occurs in the RES macrophages - mainly in the splenic RPMs and, to some extent, in liver Kupffer cells and bone marrow macrophages (Beaumont and Delaby, 2009; Ganz, 2012; Theurl et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Beaumont and Delaby, 2009; Ganz, 2012; Theurl et al., 2016 as support for this claim.

claim: SLC48A1 has a direct role in transporting heme from the phagolysosomal compartments to the cytosol for degradation by HMOX1.
source: Our results establish a direct role for SLC48A1 in transporting heme from the phagolysosomal compartments to the cytosol for degradation by HMOX1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the 59Fe labeling and microscopy experiments.

claim: Loss of HMOX1 causes over 90% embryonic lethality.
source: Unlike (SLC48A1) KO mice, loss of HMOX1 causes over 90% embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature cited in the introduction.

claim: In the absence of SLC48A1, high concentrations of heme is sequestered as hemozoin within the acidic phagolysosome, resulting in cellular heme tolerance.
source: Our results show that in the absence of SLC48A1, high concentrations of heme is sequestered as hemozoin within the acidic phagolysosome, resulting in cellular heme tolerance.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the hemozoin characterization and cell viability experiments.

claim: In the absence of HMOX1, heme accumulates within the cytosol resulting in cytotoxicity and embryonic lethality.
source: By contrast, in the absence of HMOX1, heme accumulates within the cytosol resulting in cytotoxicity and embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on the literature and the genetic cross data.

claim: Genetic epistasis would have predicted that the heme sequestration would rescue the embryonic lethality of the DKO mice.
source: Genetic epistasis would have predicted that the heme sequestration would rescue the embryonic lethality of the DKO mice.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on genetic principles.

claim: HMOX1 may have additional functions beyond heme degradation.
source: Possible explanations for this unexpected finding could be that HMOX1 has additional functions beyond heme degradation, or that the heme degradation products are required for cell differentiation and specification in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the DKO phenotype.

claim: Heme degradation products may be required for cell differentiation and specification in vivo.
source: Possible explanations for this unexpected finding could be that HMOX1 has additional functions beyond heme degradation, or that the heme degradation products are required for cell differentiation and specification in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the DKO phenotype.

claim: KO mice require a fully-operational heme degradation pathway to confer complete heme tolerance.
source: Our results support both of these explanations and further reveal that KO mice require a fully-operational heme degradation pathway to confer complete heme tolerance, as partial reduction of HMOX1 in the absence of SLC48A1 show significant embryonic lethality with severe impairment in macrophage and erythroblast maturation in the bone marrow and spleen (Figure 6F–K) raising the possibility that functional HMOX1 requires SLC48A1 on the erythrophagosomal membranes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic cross and phenotypic data.

claim: Functional HMOX1 may require SLC48A1 on the erythrophagosomal membranes.
source: Our results support both of these explanations and further reveal that KO mice require a fully-operational heme degradation pathway to confer complete heme tolerance, as partial reduction of HMOX1 in the absence of SLC48A1 show significant embryonic lethality with severe impairment in macrophage and erythroblast maturation in the bone marrow and spleen (Figure 6F–K) raising the possibility that functional HMOX1 requires SLC48A1 on the erythrophagosomal membranes.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the synthetic lethality.

claim: In the absence of SLC48A1, bioactive HMOX1 drops below the 50% expected in HMOX1 HET animals.
source: In the absence of SLC48A1, bioactive HMOX1 drops below the 50% expected in HMOX1 HET animals.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the synthetic lethality data.

claim: Blood-feeding parasites degrade hemoglobin in their digestive vacuole and accumulate heme in the form of hemozoin.
source: Blood-feeding parasites degrade hemoglobin in their digestive vacuole and accumulate heme in the form of hemozoin (Chen et al., 2001; Toh et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Chen et al., 2001; Toh et al., 2010 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemozoin formation is a heme detoxification method used to protect the parasite from heme toxicity.
source: Although the exact mechanisms of in vivo hemozoin formation are not well understood, it is generally agreed upon that hemozoin formation is a heme detoxification method used to protect the parasite from heme toxicity (Hempelmann, 2007; Toh et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hempelmann, 2007; Toh et al., 2010 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemozoin biocrystals are thought to be well-tolerated by both the parasite and subsequent host cells which ingest it.
source: Hemozoin biocrystals are thought to be well-tolerated by both the parasite and subsequent host cells which ingest it, despite some reports on the inflammatory responses towards hemozoin ingestion (Basilico et al., 2003; Schwarzer et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites Basilico et al., 2003; Schwarzer et al., 1993 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemozoin was found within LAMP1-positive intracellular vesicles, which are typically between pH 4 and 6.
source: We found hemozoin within LAMP1-positive intracellular vesicles, which are typically between pH 4 and 6 (Johnson et al., 2016; Mellman et al., 1986).
evidence: The manuscript shows confocal microscopy data (Figure 5K) and cites literature on lysosomal pH.

claim: Acidic pH appears to be a common requirement for hemozoin formation in parasitic digestive vacuoles, in vitro and in macrophages.
source: Acidic pH appears to be a common requirement for hemozoin formation in parasitic digestive vacuoles, in vitro and in macrophages (Egan et al., 2001; Shio et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Egan et al., 2001; Shio et al., 2010 as support for this claim.

claim: Hemozoin formation in mammals has not been documented prior to this study.
source: To our knowledge, hemozoin formation in mammals has not been documented prior to this study.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty.

claim: Macrophages are able to elicit a protective mechanism against high concentrations of heme by exploiting the low pH environment of lysosomes.
source: This phenomenon observed in KO spleens, livers and bone marrows suggests that macrophages are able to elicit a protective mechanism against high concentrations of heme by exploiting the low pH environment of lysosomes.

claim: KO mice have fewer RPMs, which implies that hemozoin sequestration may be incomplete or insufficient to confer complete heme tolerance.
source: It is important to note that KO mice have fewer RPMs, which implies that hemozoin sequestration may be incomplete or insufficient to confer complete heme tolerance, or that hemozoin itself could cause detrimental effects to these cells.

claim: Hemozoin in KO RES macrophages leads to tissue heme accumulation without causing major damages to tissue architecture.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of SLC48A1 in humans would lead to tolerance and protection from heme toxicity and iron overload.
